note: Written as a primer for clinicians rather than engineers, and explicit that hallucination and poor generalisation remain blockers to adoption.
title: Large language models in oncology: a review

reading.body:
Large language models show promise for supporting cancer clinicians and patients through decision assistance, medical record analysis, and emotional support, but hallucination and poor generalization currently prevent safe clinical deployment.

The applications span three areas: helping doctors make decisions and extract data from medical records, providing patients with information and psychosocial support, and accelerating research. Each domain faces the same core obstacle. Language models generate false information that sounds plausible, and they fail reliably when circumstances differ from their training data. For oncology, where errors carry life-or-death consequences, these failures are not minor technical quirks. They are blockers that hospitals cannot work around.

The review proposes embedding language models within larger systems rather than deploying them alone. Combining them with other technologies and establishing rigorous evaluation frameworks before use could reduce but not eliminate risk. This frames language models as augmentative tools, assisting clinicians rather than replacing judgment, which is the realistic near-term path if adoption happens at all.

The review does not address compute requirements, infrastructure costs, or how cancer centers would acquire or operate these systems. It focuses on technical capability and clinical safety. For institutions wondering whether to invest in language model infrastructure for oncology, the answer is conditional: only if they are prepared to wait for the underlying technology to mature and to implement careful validation before any patient-facing deployment.

explain_beginner: Cancer care involves an enormous amount of complex information, patient records, treatment guidelines, and research literature, so this review asks where AI language models could realistically help doctors, patients, and researchers working in oncology today. For doctors, the review found these systems can pull specific facts like cancer stage out of medical records quite accurately, and in some tests can generate draft treatment plans. For patients, chatbots gave answers about their diagnosis that people rated about as caring and clear as answers from actual doctors, though patients trusted the AI less as questions got more complicated. For researchers, these tools sped up scanning studies for relevant trial results. But the review is equally direct about a serious problem, these systems sometimes invent information that sounds authoritative but is false, including in one study inventing about one in eight pieces of cancer treatment information and, in another, fabricating roughly one in six of the scientific references it cited. The authors conclude these tools need more testing before hospitals rely on them directly.
explain_business: Health systems and oncology software vendors should read this review as evidence that LLM assisted tools are closer to ready for narrow, bounded tasks like extracting staging data from records, where accuracy reached 94 to 99 percent, than for open ended tasks like recommending chemotherapy regimens, where accuracy in one cited study was only 56 percent. The documented hallucination rates, including fabricated source citations found in molecular tumor board tools, are a direct patient safety and liability concern that makes unsupervised clinical use inappropriate right now under any reasonable compliance standard. The review's recommended path forward, pairing LLMs with specialized verification components and standardized evaluation frameworks such as TRIPOD+LLM and CONSORT-AI, gives buyers concrete criteria to demand from vendors, evidence of stress testing across diverse patient populations and documented hallucination rates on the specific task being sold, before considering deployment in any clinical decision support role.
explain_practitioner: This narrative review surveys LLM applications in oncology across three areas, clinician support, patient facing tools, and research acceleration, citing concrete performance figures rather than general claims. In clinician facing tasks, LLMs achieved 94 to 99 percent AUROC extracting TNM cancer staging data from electronic health records, while fine tuned models outperformed general purpose baseline LLMs on radiation oncology tasks like treatment regimen generation. In patient facing evaluations, chatbot responses to cancer questions were rated non-inferior to physician responses in some comparisons, though patient trust averaged only 3.4 out of 5 and fell as question complexity increased. In research support, a tool called SEETrials extracted trial outcome data from conference abstracts with 96 percent specificity and 94 percent sensitivity. Against this, the review documents specific failure rates other studies reported, a 12.5 percent hallucination rate generating cancer treatment information in one study, 17 percent of citations in molecular tumor board applications found fabricated in another, and only 56 percent accuracy prescribing chemotherapy regimens, leading the review's authors to recommend composite systems combining LLMs with specialized verification tools rather than relying on one general purpose model.
